rv.q: Big Fish arrives on Broadway as an earnest, family-friendly, heart-warming and mostly successful new American musical.
The show's saving grace is that it knows what it wants to be: a feel-good musical about the importance of family, told with enough theatrical razzle-dazzle to sugar-coat its bitter pill of mortality.
So when audience members around me were dabbing their eyes through the protracted finale, why did I want to take a shower?

While acknowledging that the show is about a self-consciously rambling and absurdist hero, the bloated 90-minute Act 1 threatens to derail as visual gags, projections and busy scenes - plus a book that uneasily mixes whimsy and cancer - bombard the senses....
Yet the show is hobbled by a major flaw: Andrew Lippa’s thoroughly mediocre score.
Unfortunately, Andrew Lippa’s score is a hack job stringing one banal non-tune after another.
So it's crushing to realize, early on, that this gentle, sincere, beautiful-looking show is deadly dull.
Not once did I feel that what I was seeing had been spawned by the teeming mind of Edward Bloom.
Despite a heartfelt performance by Norbert Leo Butz and a lovely score by Andrew Lippa, this adaptation of Daniel Wallace's novel never finds its theatrical footing.
But the show built around him is a pulseless bore, and you can see his shoulders sagging from carrying all that weight.
Fantasy wages war with reality in Big Fish, a delightfully old-fashioned musical based on Daniel Wallace's beloved novel.
Stroman, at the top of her game, whips this warmhearted story into a supremely imaginative and heart-tugging entertainment.
Broadway’s new musical fable, “Big Fish,” is a singing version of catch-and-release.
Where “Big Fish” gets stuck in the shallows is with its score, by Andrew Lippa (“The Addams Family”).

As the sequences of Edward's fantasies play out, however, the father-son story is frequently lost in the whimsicality rather than enhanced by it. It's only near the very end, when Will learns what Edward has accomplished and comes to appreciate the value of a man telling stories, that all the elements properly converge.
In the end, though, this Big Fish lacks the imagination or cohesion to reel you in like one of its hero's yarns.
Suddenly, they’re not archetypes anymore but rather the stars of some “Best of Broadway” theme-park show.
But the biggest fish in this pond is Butz, who splashes and swims with grace, confidence, and charisma.

The rich, gothic mise-en-scène and seamless transitions of the film are replaced with poor quality songs, a slow pace, excessive sentimentality, one-liners that consistently fail to land, a clumsy structure and an ugly set where video imagery is projected onto what look like barn doors.

cn.t: Critics find "Big Fish" visually inventive but dramatically uneven, with Norbert Leo Butz's charismatic performance praised as the show's saving grace amid complaints of a bloated structure and forgettable score.

sg.ra: For MJ the Musical's dance-heavy choreography, Center Orchestra rows A-H sit entirely in front of the mezzanine overhang (which begins at row J) and deliver head-on sightlines of the performers' feet — critical for a Michael Jackson dance biomusical. Row A seats 107-110 are frequently cited as the theatre's best, but rows C-D balance proximity with neck-angle comfort.

Because Neil Simon's orchestra is unusually deep (25 rows, A-Z) and the mezzanine overhang only starts cutting the top of the stage noticeably by row S, rows H-P give you full head-on views with no overhang effect at non-premium pricing — a specific quirk of this house's long orchestra footprint.

The mezzanine overhang is felt from row J onward and by rows S-Z it actively cuts off the top of the stage per SeatPlan's orchestra guide — a real issue for MJ the Musical, which uses tall set pieces and lifts. Unique to Neil Simon because the orchestra runs all the way to row Z, pushing rear seats deep under the overhang.

Front Center Mezzanine rows A-B give an elevated, unobstructed sweep — particularly valuable at Neil Simon because MJ the Musical uses formation choreography that reads better from above. Tripadvisor users confirm no obstruction issues at front mezz (photo cited from row A seat 103). Row A also has the best legroom in the mezzanine.

Specific Neil Simon quirk: Left and Right Mezzanine rows H and L sit directly behind railings that border the internal staircase, making legroom 'very tight' — SeatPlan calls out seats H1-7 and L9-15 by number. This is a house-specific hazard, not the generic 'Broadway legroom is tight' complaint.

Rear mezzanine at Neil Simon has a shallow rake — a specific architectural quirk noted by SeatPlan — so rows S-U feel distant and lose detail on the stage front, and the mezzanine's own underside can minor-obstruct the back-row view. For MJ's facial-expression moments in 'Man in the Mirror' numbers this is a real detriment.

Three boxes are staggered off the Left Mezzanine at Neil Simon — a specific architectural feature of this house — and SeatPlan explicitly states the viewing experience 'isn't the best' because the angle is fully side-on. Priced as premium but not worth it for a dance musical where frontal sightlines matter.
